title: Sleeping tendencies
hookLine: even a baby carries the tendencies to view, doubt and desire, asleep

cards: A baby asleep on its back, arms flung up, completely at peace. No opinions. No grudges.

No wanting anything except, eventually, milk. If anyone is free of the troubles of the mind, surely it's this tiny person. The same monk from yesterday, Māluṅkyāputta, shows up again in the very next sutta.
The Buddha asks the monks to recite five fetters, five things that bind a person. Māluṅkyāputta recites them perfectly. And the Buddha isn't pleased.

teach.b: The five are the lower fetters, in this sutta's list: the view that there's a fixed self, doubt, clinging to rules and rituals, sensual desire and ill will. Māluṅkyāputta has the list right.
What he's missing is how deep it goes. Wanderers of other sects, the Buddha says, could refute you with one simple picture.

teach.h: A TENDER INFANT ON ITS BACK.
teach.b: A young, tender infant lying on its back doesn't even have the idea of a self. How could a self-view arise in it? It has no notion of teachings, so how could it doubt them?
No notion of rules, of pleasures, of other beings to resent. And yet, he says, the underlying tendency to each of these lies within it.
The Pali word is anusaya, from a root meaning to lie down along with: the thing lying asleep under the surface. That's the turn. A fetter isn't only what you're doing right now.
You can be calm, kind, unbothered this afternoon, and the tendency to anger is still asleep in you, waiting for the right provocation. Patient all week, and then someone takes the parking spot.
The sutta isn't saying babies are bad. It's saying the roots are older than any opinion.

So later in the same sutta, the Buddha describes a practice that goes below the surface: settling the mind deeply and seeing how everything in it changes. A tendency you've watched wake up is one you can begin to know.

how: In Theravada teaching the five lower fetters and the underlying tendencies are taught as part of the stages of awakening, and meditators are trained to notice how irritation or desire arise before acting on them.

o: roots that lie asleep until something wakes them
bad habits a person picks up later in life
dreams that show what the mind really wants

games.q: the baby and the fetters: tap the pairs.
p: no idea of a self, yet the tendency
self-view, doubt, rules, desire, ill will
recited the list, missed the depth

s: the sutta says babies are wicked
it says the roots are older than our opinions, not that infants are bad.
Māluṅkyāputta got the list of five fetters wrong
he recited them correctly; the Buddha corrects his shallow grasp of them.
a tendency can be present even when it isn't active
the infant has no notion of a self, yet the tendency to self-view lies within it.

games.q: you've been calm and kind all week. does that mean the tendency to anger is gone?
o: not necessarily: it may be asleep
games.why: the sutta's point: a tendency can lie asleep, like the ones in the infant, until something wakes it.

practice: Bring to mind something small that usually irritates you, a slow line, a certain tone of voice, a notification, just long enough to feel the first flicker, a tightening in the chest or the jaw. That flicker is a tendency waking up.
Don't feed it and don't fight it; watch it, watch it settle, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sleeping tendencies. The anusayas: roots of view, doubt, desire and ill will that lie asleep in us, even in a baby, until something wakes them.

orig.note: Pali anusaya: underlying tendency, from a root meaning to lie down along with.

carryVoice: Your line: it sleeps in us. Calm today doesn't mean the root is gone. Day four hundred fifty-six, done.
